summary: Describes benefits of applications using transports with Explicit Congestion Notification, such as throughput and delay gains when routers mark packets, and challenges to deployment.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network is getting full, routers normally throw packets away, and the sender then slows down. With Explicit Congestion Notification the router instead writes a mark on the packet and passes it on, and the far end reports that mark back. This document sets out what that changes for applications and network operators, and what every device in the path has to do for it to work.

questions: what are the benefits of explicit congestion notification
what is the ecn field in ip packets
why use ecn instead of packet loss
subtitle: What routers and applications gain when congestion is signalled by marking packets instead of dropping them.

tldr.problem: Transports detect congestion by losing packets, and a lost packet is expensive: the sender slows down, data waits for the gap to be retransmitted, and the retransmission timer can fire.
tldr.mechanism: With Explicit Congestion Notification the sender marks its packets as ECN-capable, and a router that sees incipient congestion marks them CE instead of dropping them, and the receiver reports the mark back to the sender.
tldr.outcome: The packet-loss reduction is modest, about 2 percent in the example the RFC works through, but the side effects matter more: less delay waiting for retransmissions, fewer retransmission timeouts, and usable congestion control for applications that never retransmit.

today: RFC 8087 is an Informational document published in March 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it gathers the case for ECN rather than defining the mechanism, which is specified in RFC 3168, with deployment guidance in RFC 7567.

sections.title: How ECN Signals Congestion
sections.content:
Internet transports such as TCP and SCTP are implemented in endpoints and are designed to detect and react to network congestion. Congestion may be detected by the loss of an IP packet or, if Explicit Congestion Notification is enabled, by the reception of a packet with a Congestion Experienced marking in the IP header. Both are treated by transports as indications of congestion. ECN may also be used by other transports: UDP applications that provide congestion control may enable ECN when they are able to process the ECN signals correctly.

Active Queue Management is a class of techniques used by network devices to manage the size of the queues in network buffers. A network device that does not support AQM typically uses a drop-tail policy, dropping excess IP packets when its queue becomes full. The discard is treated by transport protocols as a signal that indicates congestion on the end-to-end path. Although losses are not always due to congestion, since loss may come from link corruption or receiver overrun, endpoints have to presume that all loss is potentially due to congestion and reduce their rate.

ECN lets the network signal the presence of incipient congestion without packet loss. It lets the network deliver some packets to an application that would otherwise have been dropped if the application or transport did not support ECN. This packet-loss reduction is the most obvious benefit, but it is often relatively modest, and enabling ECN also brings side effects that may be much more significant, several of which reduce latency.

The use of ECN is indicated in the ECN field, which is carried in the packet header of all IPv4 and IPv6 packets, and is set to one of four values. Not-ECT, codepoint 00, indicates a packet that is not using ECN. ECT(0), codepoint 01, and ECT(1), codepoint 10, both indicate that the transport protocol using the IP layer supports the use of ECN. The CE codepoint 11 is set by an ECN-capable network device to indicate congestion to the transport endpoint.

When an application uses a transport that enables ECN, the transport layer sets the ECT(0) or ECT(1) codepoint in the IP header of packets it sends, which tells network devices that they may mark rather than drop the ECN-capable packets. An ECN-capable network device can then signal incipient congestion at a point before the transport experiences congestion loss or high queuing delay. The marking is generally the result of an AQM algorithm, and the exact combination of AQM and ECN algorithms does not need to be known by the transport endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IP packet has two bits reserved for this. The sender sets them to say it is willing to be told about congestion. A router that finds its queue filling marks the packet with a third value and passes it on instead of throwing it away, and the receiver tells the sender what it saw. The sender then slows down, as it would have done after a loss, but nothing was actually lost.

sections.title: Throughput, Delay and Retransmission Timeouts
sections.content:
Improved throughput. ECN seeks to avoid the inefficiency of dropping data that has already made it across at least part of the network path. It can improve the throughput of an application, although this increase is often not the most significant gain. When an application uses a lightly to moderately loaded path, the number of packets dropped due to congestion is small. Using an example from a table in RFC 3649, for a standard TCP sender with an RTT of 0.1 seconds, a packet size of 1500 bytes and an average throughput of 1 Mbps, the average packet-drop ratio would be 0.02, that is 1 in 50 packets, which translates into an approximate 2 percent throughput gain if ECN is enabled. In heavy congestion, packet loss may be unavoidable with or without ECN.

Reduced head-of-line blocking. Many Internet transports provide in-order delivery of received data segments to the applications they support, and for these applications use of ECN can reduce the delay that results from packet loss. Whatever the cause of the loss, a missing packet triggers a congestion control response, and a reliable transport also triggers retransmission. For a transport providing in-order delivery, the receiver has to wait for all data that was sent ahead of a lost segment to be correctly received before it can forward any later data to the application. A loss therefore creates a delay of at least one RTT after the loss event before data can be delivered, which is called head-of-line blocking. This is the usual requirement for TCP and SCTP, while Partially Reliable SCTP, UDP and DCCP provide a transport that does not reorder. By enabling ECN, a transport continues to receive in-order data when there is incipient congestion and can pass that data to the application, which avoids the additional reordering delay in a reliable transport. The sender still has to make an appropriate congestion response, which usually means reducing the sending rate.

Reduced probability of RTO expiry. Some patterns of packet loss result in a Retransmission Timeout, which causes a sudden and significant change in the allowed rate. Because ECN gives network devices an alternative to dropping, this can reduce the probability of loss and hence the likelihood of the timer expiring. The timer detects the loss of a packet that is not followed by other packets, such as at the end of a burst of data segments or when an application becomes idle. This loss of the last segment of a traffic burst is also known as tail loss. Standard recovery methods such as Fast Recovery are often unable to recover from a tail loss, because the receiver is unaware that the lost segments were actually sent and so generates no feedback; retransmission relies on expiry of the retransmission timer, which is also used to detect a lack of forwarding along a path. Expiry of the timer results in the consequent loss of state about the path, typically resetting path estimates such as the RTT and reinitialising the congestion window, which can reduce performance until the transport adapts to the path again. An ECN-capable network device cannot eliminate the possibility of tail loss, because a drop may occur when a traffic burst exceeds the instantaneous available capacity of a buffer, or as a result of the AQM algorithm. But a device that observes incipient congestion may be expected to buffer the packets of an ECN-capable flow and set a CE mark in one or more packets rather than triggering a drop. Setting a CE mark signals incipient congestion without forcing the transport into a retransmission timeout, which reduces application-level latency and can improve the throughput for applications that send intermittent bursts of data.
sections.plainLanguage: The direct gain in throughput is small, a couple of percent in the example the RFC works through. The bigger gains are elsewhere. A connection that delivers data in order has to wait for a missing piece before it can pass on anything sent after it, so every loss costs at least one round trip of delay; a mark costs nothing. And when the last packet of a burst is lost, the sender only finds out when its retransmission timer expires, which throws away what it had learned about the path; a mark tells it straight away.

sections.title: Applications That Never Retransmit
sections.content:
A transport that enables ECN can receive timely congestion signals without retransmitting packets each time it receives a congestion signal. Some latency-critical applications do not retransmit lost packets, yet they may be able to adjust their sending rate after detecting incipient congestion. Examples are UDP-based services carrying Voice over IP, interactive video or real-time data.

The performance of many such applications degrades rapidly with increasing packet loss, so the transport or application may employ mechanisms such as packet forward error correction, data duplication or media codec error concealment to mitigate the immediate effect of congestion loss. Some of those mechanisms consume additional network capacity, some require additional processing, and some contribute additional path latency when congestion is experienced. By decoupling congestion control from loss, ECN can allow transports that support these applications to reduce their rate before the application experiences loss, which reduces the negative impact of triggering loss-hiding mechanisms and has a direct positive impact on the quality users experience.

Two further effects follow from the same mechanism. First, ECN exposes the presence of congestion on a network path to the transport and network layers, so information about incipient congestion can be collected. Recording the presence of CE-marked packets gives information about the current congestion level on a path, and a flow that only experiences CE marking and no loss implies that the sending endpoint is experiencing only congestion. A flow may also experience loss, from queue overflow, from AQM methods that protect other flows, from link corruption or in middleboxes; when a mixture of CE marking and loss is experienced, transports and measurements need to assume there is congestion, so an absence of CE marks does not indicate a path has not experienced congestion. ECN measurements are used by Congestion Exposure, while metering packet loss is harder.

Second, ECN can enable new algorithms in network devices and Internet transports. While the amount of feedback provided by a drop ought naturally to be minimized, an ECN-capable network device could provide richer and more fine-grained indication of its congestion state. The method in RFC 3168 signals once each round-trip time that CE-marked packets have been received, but a receiving endpoint may provide more detailed feedback, describing the set of received ECN codepoints or indicating each received CE-marked packet. Precise feedback about the number of CE marks encountered is supported by RTP over UDP and has been proposed for SCTP and TCP. More detailed feedback is expected to let congestion control make a more appropriate decision about how to react. Benefit has been noted when packets are CE marked early using an instantaneous queue and the receiver reports the number of marks encountered, as in Data Center TCP, which is targeted at controlled environments such as a data center and is a work in progress.
sections.plainLanguage: Live audio and video cannot resend a packet that arrived too late, so they usually hide the damage instead, and hiding costs bandwidth, processing and delay. If the sender learns about congestion before the loss happens, it can slow down first and never need to hide anything. ECN also makes congestion measurable, because a router can count the marks on a path, which it cannot do with losses.

sections.title: What Network Devices Must Do
sections.content:
For an application to use ECN the endpoints must enable it in the transport being used, and all network devices along the path must at least forward IP packets that set a non-zero ECN codepoint. ECN can be deployed incrementally in the general Internet, and it may also be deployed within a controlled environment such as a data center, where it can be tuned to the specific use case.

Early experience of using ECN across the general Internet encountered operational difficulties when the path either failed to transfer ECN-capable packets or inappropriately changed the ECN codepoints, although a recent survey reported a growing support for network paths to pass ECN codepoints.

The current IPv4 and IPv6 specifications assign usage of 2 bits in the IP header to carry the ECN codepoint. Some network devices were configured to use a routing hash that included the 8 bits forming the now deprecated Type of Service field, and the present use of this field assigns 2 of those bits to the ECN field. That is incompatible with use in a routing hash, because it could lead to packets carrying a CE mark being routed over a different path from packets carrying an ECT mark, and the resultant reordering would affect the performance of transports that are sensitive to reordering.

Not all network devices along a path need to be ECN-capable, meaning they do not have to perform CE marking, but all of them need to be configured not to drop packets solely because the ECT(0) or ECT(1) codepoints are used. Any device that does not mark ECN-capable packets can be expected to drop them under congestion, and applications that experience congestion at those devices see no benefit from enabling ECN, though they may see benefit if the congestion occurs within a device that does support ECN.

Devices that do support ECN should use an AQM algorithm that marks ECN-capable traffic, and the marking and dropping policies should be configurable independently, as recommended in RFC 7567. Devices also need to be able to forward all IP flows and treat both ECN and non-ECN traffic appropriately. A simple scheme could queue ECN-capable and non-ECN-capable flows in the same queue with marking during incipient congestion, but marked packets that remain in the queue continue to contribute to queueing delay, whereas non-ECN packets would normally be dropped under incipient congestion; that difference is one motivation for more advanced schemes and for flow isolation using scheduling.

Devices should not change the ECN codepoint in packets they forward, except to set the CE codepoint. Cases have been noted where an endpoint sends a packet with a non-zero ECN mark and the packet arrives with a zero codepoint, which could be the result of a policy that erases, or bleaches, the ECN codepoint at a network edge, sometimes to hide which equipment supports ECN. Bleaching prevents use of ECN by applications, and when ECN-capable packets are re-marked as not-ECN-capable they could be dropped by ECN-capable devices further along the path, which eliminates the advantage of using ECN. A device must not change a packet with a CE mark to a zero codepoint; if it decides not to forward the packet, it has to drop it and not bleach the marking, because a CE-marked packet has already received ECN treatment and re-marking it would hide the congestion signal from the receiving endpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: The routers have to get a few things right. They must not throw away a packet just because it is marked as willing to be told about congestion. They must not send marked packets down a different path, because that reorders the data. They must not erase the marks, and above all they must not erase the mark that says congestion, because then the far end never learns that the network is full.

sections.title: Using ECN Across the Internet
sections.content:
A receiving endpoint has to report the loss it experiences when it uses loss-based congestion control, and when ECN is enabled it must also report the presence of CE marks by feeding that congestion information back to the sending endpoint, so that the sender can react to the congestion it experienced. This mechanism has to be designed to operate robustly across a wide range of Internet path characteristics.

Use of ECN is negotiated between the endpoints before the mechanism is used. ECN was designed to allow incremental partial deployment: any network device can choose to use either ECN or some other loss-based policy, and transport and application negotiation allows the endpoints to choose whether ECN will be used to manage congestion for a particular flow.

Transports and applications need to be robust to the variety of path characteristics they encounter, and to monitor correct forwarding of ECN over the entire path and duration of a session. They have to expect heterogeneous forwarding, where some packets are marked by one device and some by another, possibly using a different AQM algorithm, or where a mixture of marking and loss-based indications is used, and they have to be robust to path changes, since a path that changes to use a middlebox that bleaches ECN codepoints affects the ability to signal congestion.

A sending endpoint can check that CE marks applied to packets it receives are indeed delivered to the remote endpoint and that appropriate feedback is provided, for example by setting a known CE codepoint on specific packets and checking whether the remote endpoint correctly reports those marks. If a sender detects persistent misuse of ECN, it needs to fall back to using loss-based recovery and congestion control. There is also a feedback problem to guard against: the receiver must not try to conceal the reception of CE-marked packets in the feedback it gives the sender, and designers are encouraged to include mechanisms that can detect this misbehaviour. If a sender detects that a receiver is not correctly providing the feedback, it needs to fall back to using loss-based recovery instead of ECN.
sections.plainLanguage: ECN is agreed between the two ends before use, so a path can be partly upgraded. The sending end has to check that the marks it sees really reach the far end and are reported back; if the path turns out to destroy the marks, or the far end hides them, the sender goes back to treating loss as the congestion signal.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces no new security considerations, and states that each RFC it lists discusses the security considerations of the specification it contains.

The document's own summary of what is needed is set out in its Section 5. Application developers should, where possible, use transports that enable ECN, and applications that directly use UDP need to provide support to implement the functions required for ECN. The application does not need to be rewritten to gain the benefits.

For network devices, the prerequisites are that a device updating the ECN field must use the IETF-specified methods, that a device must not choose a different network path solely because a packet carries a CE codepoint, that devices must be configured not to drop packets solely because the ECT codepoints are used, that an ECN-capable device should correctly update the codepoint of ECN-capable packets in the presence of incipient congestion, that devices must be able to forward both ECN-capable and not-ECN-capable flows, and that a device must not change a packet with a CE mark to a not-ECN-capable codepoint.

For network endpoints, the prerequisites are that an application should use an Internet transport that can set and receive ECN marks, that an ECN-capable transport must return feedback indicating congestion and perform an appropriate congestion response, that it should detect paths where there is persistent misuse of ECN and fall back to not sending ECT codepoints, and that mechanisms should detect and react to misbehaving receivers that fail to report CE-marked packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no security rules of its own. What it does is list what each side has to do for the mechanism to work at all, and the last two items are the important ones for safety: a sender must stop using the marks if the path or the far end misbehaves, and it must notice a receiver that tries to hide the marks.

viz.caption: THE BENEFITS OF MARKING INSTEAD OF DROPPING (RFC 8087, SECTION 2)

items.title: Improved throughput
items.text: About 2 percent in the worked example, for a lightly to moderately loaded path.

items.title: Reduced head-of-line blocking
items.text: A loss costs at least one RTT of delay in a transport that delivers in order; a mark costs none.

items.title: Reduced probability of RTO expiry
items.text: Tail loss is hard to recover from, and the timer that recovers it also discards what was learned about the path.

items.title: Applications that do not retransmit
items.text: Voice and video can slow down before loss happens, instead of hiding the damage afterwards.

items.title: Making congestion visible
items.text: Marked packets can be counted, so the congestion level on a path can be measured.

items.title: New transport mechanisms
items.text: Richer feedback about marks lets the congestion control react in a more appropriate way.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH DEVICE ON THE PATH MUST DO (RFC 8087, SECTION 5)

items.title: Do not drop marked packets
items.text: No device should drop a packet solely because it carries the ECT(0) or ECT(1) codepoint.

items.title: Keep the same path
items.text: A device must not choose a different path solely because a packet carries a CE codepoint.

items.title: Do not bleach the marks
items.text: A device must not reset a CE mark to the zero codepoint; it has to drop the packet instead.

items.title: Handle both kinds of traffic
items.text: Devices must be able to forward ECN-capable and not-ECN-capable flows.

items.title: Mark on incipient congestion
items.text: An ECN-capable device should set the CE codepoint when it sees incipient congestion.
